explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. Hebrews 9:15 says Christ is the mediator of a new covenant so that those who are called may receive the promised eternal inheritance. He died to redeem them from the transgressions committed under the first covenant. That's a gift with a very long shelf life.

Priests are all over this chapter, so I see why that one tempted you. But Hebrews 9:15 names a different gift, and it's the promised eternal inheritance. It's like my bakery being full of aprons. Nobody calls the apron the cookie.

explanations.answer: A long life in the land
explanations.explanation: A long life in the land sounds nice, friend. But Hebrews 9:15 says those who are called may receive "the promised eternal inheritance" and that's eternal, not just long. I'd trade my biggest oven for that any day.

First is right, baker. Hebrews 9:15 says Christ died to redeem them from the transgressions committed under the first covenant. The verse looks back at that covenant, and the new covenant is the one He mediates. Two covenants in one verse and you kept them straight.

Second feels natural when the verse is talking about a new covenant, friend. But Hebrews 9:15 looks backward, to transgressions committed under the first covenant. The new covenant is the one Christ mediates in that same verse. Count carefully, because I once counted a cookie tray twice and had a very confusing afternoon.

Eternal does show up in this verse, friend, but it belongs to the inheritance. Hebrews 9:15 gives "the promised eternal inheritance" to those who are called. The transgressions were committed under the first covenant. Good word, different spot, like a peppermint trying to sit where the chocolate chip goes.

explanations.answer: When the one who made it has died
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. Hebrews 9:17 says "a will does not take effect until the one who made it has died" and that it cannot be executed while he is still alive. And that's why, in verse 18, even the first covenant was not put into effect without blood.

explanations.answer: When the whole family agrees to it
explanations.explanation: Families agreeing on anything is a tall order, friend. Try getting a group chat to settle on one place to meet. But Hebrews 9:17 says a will takes effect when the one who made it has died, and a vote doesn't change that.

explanations.answer: When it is read out in public
explanations.explanation: A public reading sounds official, friend. But Hebrews 9:16 and 9:17 point to the death of the one who made the will. Verse 17 says it cannot be executed while he is still alive. A crowd and a loud voice don't change when it takes effect.

Right, baker. Hebrews 9:18 says the first covenant was not put into effect without blood. Verse 19 shows it, with Moses taking the blood of calves and goats. The will and the covenant line up right there.

Incense smells lovely, friend, though my bakery gives it a run for its money. But Hebrews 9:18 says the first covenant was not put into effect without blood. Then verse 19 has Moses taking the blood of calves and goats, and there's no incense in that verse.

Silver's shiny, friend, but nobody in this passage is counting coins. Hebrews 9:18 says the first covenant was not put into effect without blood. Then Hebrews 9:19 has Moses taking the blood of calves and goats.

explanations.answer: The scroll and all the people
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. Hebrews 9:19 says that after Moses proclaimed every commandment of the law to all the people, he took the blood of calves and goats, with water, scarlet wool and hyssop. Then he sprinkled the scroll and all the people. Nobody gets skipped in that line.

Blood on the doorframes of the houses is a real Bible moment, friend, but it's in Exodus 12:7. Here in Hebrews 9:19, Moses sprinkles the scroll and all the people. Mixing up two blood stories is easy, so no worries. Now you've got them sorted.

explanations.answer: The fields and all the flocks
explanations.explanation: Fields and flocks would be a lot of ground to cover, friend. But Hebrews 9:19 says Moses sprinkled the scroll and all the people. The fields and flocks don't show up in this verse. It's the scroll and the people themselves.

True, and it's right there in Hebrews 9:20. Moses says, "This is the blood of the covenant, which God has commanded you to keep." He says it after he sprinkles the scroll and all the people, as verse 19 tells it.

Moses wasn't doing a silent sprinkle, friend. Hebrews 9:19-20 says he sprinkled the scroll and all the people, saying, "This is the blood of the covenant, which God has commanded you to keep." So he did speak, and that's what he said. The statement on the card is true.

explanations.answer: The tabernacle and its worship vessels
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. Hebrews 9:21 says that in the same way, Moses sprinkled with blood the tabernacle and all the vessels used in worship. So the scroll and the people from verse 19 weren't the only ones. The place of worship and the vessels used in it are included too.

explanations.answer: The city gates and the walls
explanations.explanation: A whole city wall is a big swing, friend. Hebrews 9:21 names the tabernacle and all the vessels used in worship instead. Gates and walls aren't in the verse. Check the verse before you commit to a guess, like I check the oven before I commit to a batch.

explanations.answer: The tents of the twelve tribes
explanations.explanation: Every tribe's tents would be a long list, friend. I'd miss one and hear about it for years. But Hebrews 9:21 names the tabernacle and all the vessels used in worship. The tents aren't in that verse.

Right, baker. Hebrews 9:22 says that according to the law, nearly everything must be purified with blood, and "without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness." That's a heavy verse, and I think it's one to take slowly.

Rest is a lovely thing, friend, but this verse names something else. Hebrews 9:22 says nearly everything must be purified with blood according to the law, and without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness. The word the writer lands on is forgiveness. It's a heavy verse, so I'll leave it there.

Wisdom is a good thing, friend, but it isn't the word in this verse. Hebrews 9:22 says that without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness. That's a heavy verse, so I'll keep it simple. The word is forgiveness.

That's the word, baker. Hebrews 9:23 says the copies of the heavenly things had to be purified with these sacrifices, but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these. Copies on one side, heavenly things on the other. The word better marks the difference.

Smaller is a sensible guess, friend, since copies are often smaller than the real thing. But Hebrews 9:23 says the heavenly things themselves are purified with better sacrifices than these. The verse measures by better, not by size. Same with my cookies, because quality beats how many fit on the tray.

Older does fit with the first covenant, friend, but it isn't the word in this verse. Hebrews 9:23 says the heavenly things themselves are purified with better sacrifices than these. Old is great for family recipes. Here, the word is better.

Right, baker. Hebrews 9:24 says Christ did not enter a man-made copy of the true sanctuary, but He entered heaven itself. He goes there to appear on our behalf in the presence of God. Copy out, real thing in.

Mount Sinai is a famous mountain, friend, but it's not on this verse's map. Hebrews 9:24 sends Christ to heaven itself, where He appears on our behalf in the presence of God. So pick a different address.
Eden is a lovely place to know about, friend, but it isn't the answer here. Hebrews 9:24 says Christ entered heaven itself, in the presence of God. Same question, different address.
True, baker. Hebrews 9:24 says Christ entered heaven itself, now to appear on our behalf in the presence of God. On our behalf means for us. So the verse has Him in the presence of God for our sake.
That one says no, friend, but Hebrews 9:24 says yes. Christ entered heaven itself, now to appear on our behalf in the presence of God. So the statement on the card is true, and it's good news for us.

It's tempting to match Christ to the high priest, friend, since they sit side by side in the verse. But Hebrews 9:25 says He did not enter heaven to offer Himself "again and again," as the high priest enters the Most Holy Place every year with blood that is not his own. The yearly trips belong to the high priest. Hebrews 9:26 says Christ has appeared once for all.

False is right, baker. Hebrews 9:25 says He did not enter heaven to offer Himself again and again, as the high priest enters the Most Holy Place every year with blood that is not his own. Then verse 26 says He has appeared once for all at the end of the ages. Once is a lot different from every year.

explanations.answer: He would have suffered over and over since the world began
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. Hebrews 9:26 says that otherwise, Christ would have had to suffer repeatedly since the foundation of the world. That's heavy to think about, so I'll say it plainly. But the verse goes on to say He has appeared once for all at the end of the ages to do away with sin by the sacrifice of Himself.

explanations.answer: Moses would have sprinkled the people every single year
explanations.explanation: Moses and his sprinkling belong to the earlier verses, friend, back in Hebrews 9:19. This question is about what Christ would have had to go through. Hebrews 9:26 says He would have had to suffer repeatedly since the foundation of the world. Let's keep the answer in Christ's lane.

explanations.answer: The tabernacle would have had to be rebuilt in heaven
explanations.explanation: A tabernacle rebuilt in heaven sounds like a big construction job, friend. But Hebrews 9:24 says Christ entered heaven itself, not a man-made copy. And Hebrews 9:26 says that otherwise He would have had to suffer repeatedly since the foundation of the world. No building crew in this verse.

Right, baker. Hebrews 9:27 says man is appointed to die once, and Hebrews 9:28 says Christ was offered once to bear the sins of many. The writer lines the two onces up with that "just as" and "so also."
Prayers are precious, friend, but the verse names something else. Hebrews 9:28 says Christ was offered once to bear the sins of many. What He bears there is sins.

Praises are wonderful, friend, and I like them as much as the next stamper. But Hebrews 9:28 says Christ was offered once to bear the sins of many. The verse says sins, so that's the word for the blank.

Not this time, friend. Hebrews 9:28 says He will appear a second time, "not to bear sin, but to bring salvation to those who eagerly await Him." Bearing sin belongs to the once, when He was offered for many. The card has it flipped around, so the statement is false.

Right, baker. Hebrews 9:28 says He will appear a second time, "not to bear sin, but to bring salvation to those who eagerly await Him." The bearing of sin was the once, and the second appearance is about salvation. The verse doesn't say when, and neither do I. Matthew 24:36 says only the Father knows the day and hour, so I keep my ovens warm.

Right, baker. Hebrews 9:28 says He will bring salvation to those who eagerly await Him. Eagerly is the word, like standing by the oven in the last thirty seconds and not even pretending to do something else. It's a verse for the ones watching and waiting.

explanations.answer: The priests who served the tabernacle
explanations.explanation: Priests fill this chapter, friend, so I get why they came to mind. But Hebrews 9:28 says salvation comes to those who eagerly await Him. The priests who served the tabernacle aren't named in that verse.

explanations.answer: Everyone who kept the law of Moses
explanations.explanation: Keeping the law of Moses sounds like a solid answer, friend. But Hebrews 9:28 describes those who eagerly await Him, and the law of Moses isn't named there. The verse says those who eagerly await Him, so that's the line I'm sticking to.
